Traveller: The Musical Journey of Bruce Beresford
David: It was only a dream, father.
Saul: Well, if it was a dream, send in my musician—let me dream on.
—King David (directed by Bruce Beresford, 1985)
Music and film have had a long love affair. Today, it’s hard to imagine a movie without a score or musical soundtrack. But some notable films have done without: Fritz Lang’s M (1931), Alfred Hitchcock’s Rope (1948) and The Birds (1963), Ingmar Bergman’s Winter Light (1963), Sidney Lumet’s Dog Day Afternoon (1975) and Network (1976), and in this century, the Coen Brothers’ No Country for Old Men (2007).
Hitchcock, who cut his teeth in the silent film era, always insisted on the primacy of “pure film”: “If it’s a good movie, the sound could go off and the audience would still have a perfectly clear idea of what was going on.”
Live piano accompanied the first Lumière film in 1895, and cinemas in the silent era often employed pianists or organists. Sometimes orchestras played classical music…
